- If sentiment is negative or shows early bearish signals, reduce forecast slope or shift downward by 2–5% to account for risk aversion.  
- If model shows steady upward trend with no recent dip, check for overconfidence — especially if sentiment is neutral or mildly bullish; cap growth to avoid overshoot.  
- After sharp price spikes (e.g., >5% in 1–2 days), model often overcorrects — reduce forecast slope for next 3–5 days to allow for mean reversion.  
- If true outcome shows strong downward trend after a peak, model may lag — adjust forecast to reflect earlier decline, especially if sentiment turns bearish.  
- When sentiment is bullish (e.g., >0.5) and model is flat or rising slowly, consider slight upward bias — but cap at 3–5% above recent high to avoid overestimating momentum.  
- If sentiment is neutral or mixed, model should not overfit to recent history — use 3–5 day moving average or median of recent 10–15 days to avoid false momentum.  
- If true outcome deviates sharply from model in first 5–7 days, treat as “early correction” — adjust forecast downward by 1–3% for next 3–5 days to reflect sentiment lag.  
- Avoid forecasting linear trends when sentiment shows volatility — use exponential decay or stepwise adjustments to reflect sentiment shifts.
